# The Lantern at Meihua Bridge

---

The magistrate had been dead for three days before anyone noticed.

It was not that the people of Qinghe were unobservant. It was that Magistrate Shen continued to hold court each morning, continued to sign documents with his red-inked brush, continued to take his evening tea on the western balcony overlooking the canal. His servant, Old Wu, brought him meals that went uneaten, but Old Wu had served three magistrates before this one, and he had learned long ago not to ask questions of powerful men.

It was the flies that finally told the truth. They gathered at the closed door of the magistrate's private chamber in a humming black curtain, and when the prefect's men finally broke the door from its frame, they found Magistrate Shen on his bed, three days gone into rot, his face frozen in an expression of such perfect terror that two of the soldiers had to be relieved and sent to the courtyard to be sick.

But the question remained — if the magistrate had been dead in his chamber since the night of the autumn moon, who had been sitting at his bench each morning, dispensing justice in his name?

---

I will tell you what I know. My name is Zhou Ping, and I was a clerk in the magistrate's court for eleven years. I kept records. I copied testimony. I have no gift for poetry or embellishment, only a steady hand and an honest memory, and I tell you now that what I witnessed was real.

It began with the woman on Meihua Bridge.

Meihua Bridge crossed the narrowest point of the old canal on the eastern edge of town, where the water ran black and still beneath a canopy of plum trees. It had not been used in years — not since the new stone bridge was built further south — and the wooden planks had grown soft and treacherous with damp. Children were warned away from it. Even the beggars avoided it after dark.

But in the eighth month of the thirty-second year of the Kangxi Emperor's reign, people began to see a woman standing at the center of the bridge at night.

She was always described the same way: tall, dressed in white mourning clothes, holding a paper lantern that burned with a pale blue flame. Her hair was unbound and hung past her waist like a black waterfall. Her face, those who dared to look said, was beautiful — but wrong somehow. Too still. Like a painting of a face rather than a face itself.

She never spoke. She never moved. She simply stood and held her lantern over the water, as though searching for something in the dark below.

The first person to report her was a fisherman named Gao, who had been checking his eel traps downstream. He told anyone who would listen, and most people would not. The second was a widow who lived in the house nearest the bridge and swore she could see the blue light from her window every night between the second and third watch. The third was a boy of fourteen who had gone to the bridge on a dare and came back unable to speak. He did not recover his voice for a month, and when he did, he would only say: *She looked at me. She looked at me and I saw that she had no eyes.*

I recorded each of these accounts because that was my duty. Magistrate Shen read them with the detached interest he applied to all things, then set them aside.

"Superstition," he said. "The canal district attracts a low quality of person. Low persons see low things."

This was before he died, of course.

---

I must now tell you about the canal, and the thing that had happened there six months prior, though it shames me and shames the memory of the court I served.

In the spring of that year, a young woman named Fan Yulian had come before Magistrate Shen to plead a case against a merchant named Hou Desheng. She claimed that Hou had promised her marriage, had taken her virtue, and had then cast her aside when a wealthier match was arranged. She begged the magistrate for justice.

I remember her clearly. She wore a blue cotton jacket, faded but clean. Her hands trembled when she knelt. She was not beautiful in the way that moves poets, but there was a clarity in her face, a kind of fierce dignity that made it difficult to look away.

Magistrate Shen heard her case. He examined the evidence. And then he ruled in favor of Hou Desheng, because Hou Desheng had sent to the magistrate's residence, three nights before the hearing, a lacquer box containing two hundred taels of silver and a piece of Hetian jade carved in the shape of a qilin.

I know this because I saw the box. I said nothing because I was a clerk, and clerks who speak do not remain clerks for long. They become corpses.

Fan Yulian received the judgment in silence. She did not weep. She did not protest. She stood, thanked the magistrate for his time with a bow so correct it bordered on mockery, and walked out of the courtroom.

That night, her body was pulled from the canal beneath Meihua Bridge. She had filled her sleeves with stones.

I recorded this too.

---

After the sightings began, Magistrate Shen ordered the bridge watched, but the two soldiers he assigned to the task refused to return after the first night. They would not say what they had seen. They accepted their punishment — twenty strokes each — in silence, which told me more than any testimony could. A man will suffer twenty strokes rather than go back to a place only when what waits at that place is worse than twenty strokes.

Magistrate Shen then ordered the bridge torn down. A work crew was dispatched at dawn. By noon, they had removed perhaps a third of the planks when the foreman slipped and fell into the canal. The water there was no more than waist-deep, but the foreman went under and did not resurface. When they dragged him out with hooked poles, they found his arms rigid at his sides, his legs pressed together, his body straight and stiff as a board — as though something had pulled him down by the feet and held him there. The expression on his face was the same one they would later find on the magistrate.

The work crew refused to continue. The bridge remained.

---

It was around this time that I began to notice changes in the magistrate himself.

He had always been a hard man — not cruel by nature, I think, but indifferent, which is its own species of cruelty. He ate well, slept well, judged cases with efficiency and went home to his concubines. The bribe from Hou Desheng was not the first he had accepted and would not have been the last.

But in the weeks after the sightings began, his appetite vanished. His face grew sallow. He started at small sounds — the creak of a door, the scratch of my brush on paper. Twice I saw him staring at an empty corner of the courtroom with an expression I had never seen him wear before and could not immediately identify.

It was fear.

One evening, as I was finishing the day's records, he called me to his bench. The courtroom was empty. The evening light came through the high windows in dusty orange bars.

"Zhou Ping," he said. "You are a man of letters. Tell me — the old texts speak of gui, of hungry ghosts who return to settle debts. Do you believe such things are real?"

I chose my words carefully. "The Zuozhuan records many such instances, Your Honor. As does the Soushenji. Whether they are literal truths or moral illustrations, I cannot say."

"Moral illustrations," he repeated, and something that might have been a laugh came from his throat, though it sounded more like a cough. "Yes. That is the comfortable answer."

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, very softly, as though speaking to himself: "She comes to my window now. Every night. She stands outside and holds up that lantern, and the light comes through the shutters and falls across my bed in the shape of a hand. I have had the shutters nailed. I have had talismans pasted over every door. She comes regardless."

He looked at me, and I saw that his eyes were rimmed with red, and that the flesh beneath them had gone dark as a bruise.

"The light is cold, Zhou Ping. It is the coldest thing I have ever felt."

I did not know what to say. I bowed and left.

That was the last time I spoke to Magistrate Shen alive.

---

Three nights later, the servants heard nothing. No cry. No struggle. Old Wu brought the morning tea to the magistrate's private chamber and found the door locked from the inside. He assumed the magistrate wished to sleep late and did not press the matter.

But someone — *something* — emerged from the magistrate's study that morning, dressed in his robes, wearing his cap, and took his seat at the bench.

I was there. I sat at my clerk's desk not ten feet away. And I tell you that the thing in the magistrate's chair looked like Magistrate Shen in every particular — the same square face, the same heavy brows, the same ink-stained fingers resting on the bench.

But it was not him.

I knew this the way a dog knows thunder is coming — not through reason, but through something older and deeper, a wrongness that settled in my bones. The air in the courtroom had changed. It smelled of canal water and plum blossoms.

And the judgments — the judgments were different.

The first case that morning involved a landlord who had cheated a tenant farmer of his harvest. Under the real Magistrate Shen, the landlord would have paid a modest fine, if that. The thing in the chair ordered the landlord to return double the harvest's value and to kneel before the farmer in open court and beg forgiveness. The landlord sputtered and protested. The thing in the chair looked at him, and the landlord went silent and white and knelt so quickly his knees cracked against the stone floor.

The second case involved a brothel keeper accused of holding a girl against her will. The thing in the chair freed the girl and ordered the brothel keeper's hands broken.

The third case was a debt dispute. The fourth was a matter of stolen goods. In each, the thing in the chair ruled with a terrible, swift precision that favored the wronged and punished the wicked with a severity that Magistrate Shen had never once displayed.

I recorded every judgment. My hands were shaking, but I recorded them.

During the noon recess, I worked up the courage to look — truly look — at the face of the thing in the chair. It sat perfectly still, hands folded, eyes forward. It did not blink. It did not breathe. And in the hollow light of the courtroom, I saw that its shadow fell in the wrong direction — toward the light, not away from it — and that where its shadow touched the floor, frost had formed in thin white patterns, like the veins of a leaf.

I looked at its eyes.

They were not Magistrate Shen's eyes.

They were dark and flat and deep, like water in a well, and they held a grief so vast and so old that I felt my own heart clench in my chest. I understood then that I was not looking at a demon or a monster. I was looking at someone who had been denied justice in life and had returned from death to find it — not only for herself, but for every soul who had stood in that courtroom and been turned away.

The thing in the chair turned its head and looked at me.

I could not move. I could not breathe. The cold washed over me like river water, and in that cold I heard — not with my ears but somewhere behind them — a voice.

*Are you afraid?*

I was. God of heaven, I was.

*Good. The ones who were not afraid were always the most dangerous.*

Then the cold released me, and the thing in the chair turned away, and the afternoon cases were called.

---

This continued for three days.

For three days, the dead woman held court in the body of the man who had failed her, and she dispensed a justice so pure and so merciless that the people of Qinghe began to whisper that Magistrate Shen had been transformed — that he had found religion, or conscience, or fear of heaven. They did not know he was rotting behind a locked door while something wore his face.

On the third evening, when the flies finally brought the truth, the prefect's men searched the entire compound. The courtroom was empty. The magistrate's robes and cap were folded neatly on the bench, as though someone had undressed with great care and laid everything in its proper place.

On the bench beside the robes, they found a single object: a blue cotton jacket, faded but clean, folded into a perfect square.

I recognized it at once.

---

The bridge was torn down the following week. No one interfered. The canal was dredged, and in the mud beneath the place where the bridge had stood, they found a stone — a single smooth river stone, the kind a woman might slip into her sleeve. Carved into its surface, in characters so small you had to hold it to the light to read them, were two words:

*记住*

*Remember.*

---

There was an investigation, of course. The prefect sent officials. Hou Desheng, the merchant who had ruined Fan Yulian, was arrested on unrelated charges of fraud and died in prison before his trial. The lacquer box with its silver and jade was found in Magistrate Shen's private stores, and the full account of his corruption was entered into the record.

A new magistrate was appointed. He was, by all accounts, scrupulously fair. Whether this was by nature or by fear, I cannot say.

As for me, I remained at my desk. I kept records. I copied testimony. But I kept the stone from the canal in my sleeve, and on nights when the plum trees bloomed along the water, I sometimes walked to the place where Meihua Bridge had stood and set a stick of incense at the water's edge.

The woman in white was never seen again.

But on certain autumn nights, when the moon was full and the canal lay still and dark as polished bronze, the people who lived nearby said they could see a pale blue light moving slowly beneath the surface of the water — not searching anymore, but drifting, gently, like a lantern carried by someone who had finally found what she was looking for and was at last, at last, going home.

---

*I have set this account down faithfully in the thirty-third year of the Kangxi Emperor's reign. Let those who read it remember that the dead have long memories, and that justice, once denied, does not sleep. It only waits.*

*— Zhou Ping, Clerk of the Qinghe Magistrate's Court*
